Uxorial means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a wife." Whenever something is described as uxorial, it belongs to, comes from, or is typical of a wife — her role, her behavior, her feelings, or her position within a marriage.

A useful parallel: just as "maternal" means relating to a mother and "paternal" means relating to a father, uxorial means relating to a wife. It uses the wife as the central reference point.
What this looks like in practice

In a sentence like "She fulfilled her uxorial duties with grace," uxorial simply means the duties that come with being a wife. In "His will reflected deep uxorial affection," it means affection directed toward or associated with his wife. In "She shed her uxorial identity after the divorce," it means her identity as a wife. In every case, the word is just pointing you back to the wife — her role, her experience, her status.

Importantly, uxorial is a neutral word. It carries no praise or criticism on its own. It doesn't say whether a wife's role is good or bad, important or trivial. It simply points to the wife as the reference point.

This is the single most important distinction to learn. There's a closely related word, uxorious (ending in "-ious" instead of "-ial"), and the two are frequently mixed up. Uxorious describes a husband who is excessively, even weakly, devoted to his wife — a man who submits to her every wish to a degree that others might find embarrassing or ridiculous. It carries a gently mocking, slightly negative tone.

The split is clean: uxorial describes things relating to a wife (neutral descriptor), while uxorious describes a husband who is overly doting (subtly critical). One is about the wife; the other is about how a husband behaves toward her.
Who uses this word, and where

Uxorial is a formal, literary word — you will never hear it at a dinner table or in casual conversation. It lives in legal documents (discussing a wife's rights, duties, or entitlements in historical or formal contexts), in academic writing about marriage in sociology, anthropology, and history, and in literary or classic fiction. If you use it correctly in writing, it immediately signals a precise and sophisticated vocabulary.

Uxorial is not about women in general, or about female partners broadly. It is specifically about a wife — a woman in the formal, recognized role of marriage. The word carries that institutional weight.

Every single time you see or hear the word uxorial, just think: "This is about the wife." Her role. Her duties. Her feelings. Her position. The word is simply the adjective that belongs to her. That one sentence captures everything the word does.
